To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) The standard pipeline for OTU clustering and annotation using sequence similarity is not reliable.

(1) the standard approach to clustering 16S sequences is not sufficient to accurately represent microbial communities; and (2) we have developed a new clustering algorithm based on a novel similarity metric, called ‘Sequence Variability’ (SV), that is better able to accurately represent microbial community structure.

(1) pairwise alignment-based clustering of 16S sequences is problematic; (2) the resulting OTUs are poorly clustered; (3) the use of pairwise alignment-based clustering results in a large number of spurious OTUs; and (4) the resulting OTU annotations are inaccurate.

the development of new computational methods to address the challenges associated with 16S ampilicon analysis.

the traditional approach for OTU clustering based upon percent similarity is not sufficient and should be replaced with a more rigorous clustering technique.
clustering of amplicons is a necessary evil, but it is not the best solution.
the standard approach to 16S ampilicon analysis using OTUs is not a good idea.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the current standard approach of OTU clustering is not sufficient for the accurate analysis of 16S data.
the current standard pipeline for 18S amplicon clustering is insufficient.
the standard approach to clustering sequences using a percent sequence similarity cut-off is insufficient for 16S rDNA sequence analysis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
clustering methods should be chosen based on the biological question at hand and that the choice of clustering method is not a trivial decision.
the standard clustering approach is not sufficient to capture the true taxonomic composition of a microbial sample.
clustering methods that do not rely on pairwise sequence alignments should be considered.
